passages.title: Mexican transmission · Document 39, opening and nested note, transcribed pp.44–45
passages.text: Mr. Secretary: I have the honor to transcribe to your excellency the following note, which the Secretary of Foreign Relations of my country has been pleased to write to me: Querétaro, February 11, 1917. Señor Ramón P. De Negri, Washington, D. C.: Please transcribe to the most excellent the Minister of Foreign Relations of that country the following note: By direction of Citizen Venustiano Carranza, First Chief of the Constitutionalist Army, in charge of the executive power of the Mexican nation, I have the honor of addressing to your excellency the following note, which the above-named high mandatory has seen fit to send to the neutral countries:
passages.context: De Negri transcribes Aguilar, writing by Carranza’s direction; FRUS labels the record Translation without naming a translator. The outer date is February 12 and the nested note February 11.

passages.title: Mexican proposal · Document 39, two proposal paragraphs, transcribed pp.45–46
passages.text: To that end the Government of Mexico, within the bounds of the strictest respect due to the sovereignty of the warring countries, inspired by the highest humanitarian sentiments, and also actuated by the sentiment of self-conservation and defense, takes the liberty of proposing to your excellency’s Government, as it is proposing to all the other neutral governments, that the groups of contending powers be invited, in common accord and on the basis of absolutely perfect equality on either side, to bring this war to an end either by their own effort or by availing themselves of the good offices of friendly mediation of all the countries which Would jointly extend that invitation. If within a reasonable term peace could not be restored by this means, the neutral countries would then take the necessary measures to reduce the conflagration to its narrowest limit, by refusing any kind of implements to the belligerents and suspending commercial relations with the warring nations until the said conflagration shall have been smothered.
passages.context: A stated proposal to neutral governments: invite peace or mediation, then suspend supplies and trade if peace does not follow. It does not answer the German alliance proposal.

passages.title: Mexican cooperation · Document 39, cooperation and named neutral states, transcribed p.46
passages.text: The Government of Mexico understands that no neutral nation, no matter how mighty, could singly take a step of this character, and that the measure can only be brought to a successful issue through the cooperation of the neutral governments wielding the greatest international influence with the belligerent nations. It is specially incumbent on the United States, Argentina, Brazil, and Chile in America; Spain, Sweden, and Norway in Europe, as being more influential and freer to arrive at a decision toward the belligerents, to father an initiative which is none the less worthy of thorough study and earnest consideration for its coming from a nation which is supposed to be weakened at present and therefore incapable of any effective international effort.
passages.context: The note presents concerted neutral action and resists the assumption of Mexican incapacity. This is diplomatic self-presentation, not a demonstrated policy outcome.

passages.title: Reported nonreceipt · Document 300, first body paragraph, transcribed p.238
passages.text: He said that Mexico had not received up to the present time from Germany any proposition whatever of alliance;
passages.context: Fletcher reports Carranza’s assertion of nonreceipt. A report of a denial does not establish whether a proposal had actually arrived.

passages.title: Reported conditional answer · Document 300, first body paragraph, transcribed p.239
passages.text: In answer to my direct question as to his attitude in case Germany should propose an alliance, he said that Mexico desires to avoid becoming involved in the war and again referred to his note, but he avoided saying directly that such a proposition would be rejected.
passages.context: Fletcher reports an answer to a hypothetical alliance question and characterizes it as avoiding direct rejection; this is not a signed Mexican rejection.

passages.title: Ambassador inference · Document 300, first body paragraph, transcribed p.239
passages.text: Personally I do not think Mexico would under present circumstances accept alliance referred to but I think First Chief wishes withhold categorical statement to that effect in the hope of inducing our Government to accept his peace proposals or a peace conference of neutrals.
passages.context: The ambassador explicitly marks his prediction and explanation of Carranza’s motive as his own belief. Keep this distinct from reported speech and from evidence of actual decisions.

passages.title: Us response · Document 59, response to the peace invitation, transcribed p.68
passages.text: In these circumstances, all of which were existent when the note under acknowledgment was received, the Government of the United States finds itself, greatly to its regret and contrary to its desires, in a position which precludes it from participating at the present time in the proposal of General Carranza that the neutral governments jointly extend an invitation to the belligerent countries to bring the war to an end either by their own effort or by availing themselves of the good offices or friendly mediation of neutral countries.
passages.context: Lansing communicates the United States’ inability to join the invitation at that time. It is a US response to Mexican peace proposals, not Mexico’s response to Germany.

passages.title: Us trade position · Document 59, response to the trade proposal, transcribed p.68
passages.text: Believing that this position of the United States is based upon sound principles of international law and is consonant with the established practice of nations, the President directs me to say that he can not bring himself to consider such a modification of these principles or of this practice as compliance with General Carranza’s proposal to suspend commercial relations with the warring nations would entail.
passages.context: The US response invokes its stated legal and policy position against suspending commercial relations; the packet does not adjudicate that legal argument.

claims.text: A proposed neutral policy is evidence of a stated position, not its successful execution.
claims.qualification: Diplomatic self-presentation is not a demonstrated outcome.

claims.text: Fletcher reports an assertion of nonreceipt; that report alone does not settle actual receipt.
claims.qualification: Keep witness, reported speaker and proposition distinct.

context: Carranza’s direction, Aguilar’s note, De Negri’s transmission, the unnamed English translation and the later FRUS edition form different layers of the record.

Repeated mentions of one diplomatic initiative do not automatically create independent corroboration. Fletcher’s prediction is marked as his belief.

What this exploration can establish
